nodes.name: Host-guest encapsulation
nodes.procedure: The Y(acac)3@ZIF-8 precursor was initially fabricated following the reported host–guest strategy. During this process, Zn-based zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF-8) nanocrystals were employed as hosts to trap yttrium acetylacetonate (Y(acac)3) guest molecules.
nodes.source_text: The synthetic route for the Ru–YNC is depicted in Fig. 1(a). Briefly, the Y(acac)3@ZIF-8 precursor was initially fabricated following the reported host–guest strategy.

nodes.name: Pyrolysis and acid etching
nodes.procedure: Subsequently, the Y(acac)3@ZIF-8 precursor underwent the pyrolysis and acid etching treatment to prepare the YNC, which was constituted of isolated Y SAs immobilized on a N-doped carbon support. The Zn atoms in the Y(acac)3@ZIF-8 precursor were essentially evaporated during the pyrolysis process at 950 °C, and further completely removed by the subsequent acid etching treatment owing to the weak Zn–N coordination in acidic media.

nodes.name: Impregnation-reduction
nodes.procedure: The Ru–YNC that comprises ultrasmall Ru clusters anchored on the YNC support was ultimately synthesized via an impregnation-reduction method, which involved the adsorption of Ru3+ ions from 0.5 mg/mL RuCl3 aqueous solution and annealing under a reducing atmosphere.
nodes.source_text: The Ru–YNC that comprises ultrasmall Ru clusters anchored on the YNC support was ultimately synthesized via an impregnation-reduction method, which involved the adsorption of Ru3+ ions and annealing under a reducing atmosphere.

nodes.name: Direct ZIF-8 pyrolysis
nodes.procedure: For comparison, the Ru–NC without Y SAs was also prepared through the similar procedure except for employing the N-doped carbon support directly pyrolyzed from the ZIF-8 precursor.
nodes.source_text: For comparison, the Ru–NC without Y SAs was also prepared through the similar procedure except for employing the N-doped carbon support directly pyrolyzed from the ZIF-8 precursor.

nodes.description: Alkaline HER LSV performance in 1.0 M KOH using three-electrode system
nodes.source_text: The electrochemical alkaline HER performance of the Ru–YNC was evaluated in N₂-saturated 1.0 M KOH solution using a standard three-electrode system... the linear scanning voltammetry (LSV) curves with 95% iR-correction exhibit extremely low overpotentials of 22 and 109 mV at current densities of 10 and 100 mA cm⁻² for the Ru–YNC... the Tafel slope of the Ru–YNC is only 39 mV dec⁻¹... the Ru–YNC catalyst delivers an outstanding noble metal mass activity of 17.79 A mg_noble metal⁻¹ at -0.1 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE)

nodes.description: AEMWE electrolyzer performance with Ru–YNC cathode and NiFe-LDH anode
nodes.source_text: an AEMWE electrolyzer using the Ru–YNC as the cathode and the homemade NiFe layered double hydroxide (NiFe-LDH) as the anode was constructed... All the AEMWE electrolyzers were operated at 80 °C in 1.0 M KOH solution separated by a Sustainion® X37-50 anion exchange membrane... the Ru–YNC||NiFe-LDH electrolyzer delivers current densities of 500 and 1000 mA cm⁻² at lower cell voltages of 1.78 and 1.87 V... the noble metal mass activity of the Ru–YNC||NiFe-LDH electrolyzer with a Ru loading of only 0.019 mg cm⁻² can reach 52.07 A mg_Ru⁻¹ at a cell voltage of 1.87 V... remarkable stability over 1000 h at an industrial-level current density of 500 mA cm⁻² with a degradation rate as low as 40 μV h⁻¹
the chronopotentiometry measurement of the Ru–YNC was performed at a constant current density of 10 mA cm⁻². It exhibits a negligible decay after 200 h
the chronopotentiometry measurement of the Ru–YNC under harsher conditions of 100 mA cm⁻² for 24 h was also conducted, which shows that the overpotential increases by merely 4 mV
The polarization curve of the Ru–YNC after enduring 10 000 CV cycles only shows slightly negative shifts of 1, 3, and 10 mV at current densities of 10, 100 and 200 mA cm⁻², respectively

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM images show well-dispersed Ru clusters with average size 2.2 nm in Ru–YNC.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The HAADF-STEM images of the Ru–YNC exhibit numerous well-dispersed metal clusters with an average particle size of only 2.2 nm (Fig. 1(b) and (c)).

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM discloses lattice fringes of 0.214 nm in Ru clusters, assigned to (002) plane of hcp Ru.
nodes.evidence_snippet: the high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images disclose that the individual metal cluster presents lattice fringes with a spacing of 0.214 nm... assigned to the (002) plane of hexagonal close-packed (hcp) Ru.

properties.description: Orange and pink spheres representing Ru atoms

nodes.characterization_summary: AC-HAADF-STEM visualizes coexistence of Ru clusters and Y single atoms; interplanar spacings match (002) plane of hcp Ru.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As illustrated in Fig. 1(e), the enlarged atomic-scale resolution AC-HAADF-STEM image demonstrates that the atomic arrangements and interplanar spacings of individual metal clusters match well with the (002) plane of the hcp Ru... the coexistence of Ru clusters and Y SAs (encircled by red circles) is distinctly visualized.

nodes.characterization_summary: EDX elemental mapping shows Ru concentrated on clusters, Y evenly distributed on N-doped carbon support.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 1(g), the Ru signal is mainly concentrated on monodispersed metal clusters, while the Y signal is evenly distributed throughout the N-doped carbon support.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru content 0.95 wt% and Y content 0.91 wt% in Ru–YNC.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The specific contents of Ru and Y elements in the Ru–YNC were determined to be 0.95 and 0.91 wt.%, respectively, by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry (ICP-AES).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru–YNC shows no XRD peaks for hcp Ru due to ultrasmall cluster size; Ru–NC shows slight peak at 44° for (101) hcp Ru.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Remarkably, no XRD diffraction peaks ascribed to the hcp Ru are detected in the Ru–YNC due to the ultrasmall size... Ru–NC containing Ru clusters with an average size of 3.1 nm exhibits a slight XRD peak at approximately 44° corresponding to the (101) plane of the hcp Ru.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru 3p XPS shows Ru⁰ at 462.4/484.6 eV and Ru⁴⁺ at 464.3/486.7 eV in Ru–YNC with negative shift vs Ru–NC; Y 3d shows positive shift.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Ru species in the Ru–YNC predominantly comprise metallic Ru⁰ (3p3/2 and 3p1/2 of 462.4 and 484.6 eV...) Ru⁴⁺ 3p3/2 and 3p1/2 of 464.3 and 486.7 eV... peak positions of Ru 3p in the Ru–YNC shift towards lower binding energies relative to those of the Ru–NC.

properties.description: XPS spectrum showing Y 3d peaks for YNC
XPS spectrum showing Y 3d peaks for Ru-YNC with Y6+ and Y+

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru K-edge XANES shows reduced oxidation state in Ru–YNC vs Ru–NC; Y K-edge shows positive shift vs YNC, confirming electron transfer from Y to Ru.
nodes.evidence_snippet: the Ru K-edge XANES spectra reveal that the edge energy of the Ru–YNC is close to that of the Ru foil (Ru0) and exhibits a negative shift relative to that of the Ru–NC... a slightly positive shift in the edge energy of the Ru–YNC compared with that of the YNC is observed in the Y K-edge XANES spectra.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru K-edge EXAFS shows Ru–Ru at 2.48 Å (CN=5.7) and Ru–N at 1.58 Å (CN=1.5); Y K-edge shows Y–N at 1.71 Å (CN≈4), confirming atomic dispersion of Y.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In the Ru K-edge EXAFS spectra, both the Ru–YNC and Ru–NC exhibit the predominant scattering peaks located at about 2.48 Å... Regarding the Y K-edge EXAFS spectra... The predominant peak at about 1.71 Å is ascribed to the scattering path of first-shell Y–N coordination.
